newsitem.title: USA: Clinton appeals for donations he would ban.
newsitem.headline: Clinton appeals for donations he would ban.

text.p: A week after asking federal regulators to prohibit unlimited "soft money" contributions to political parties, President Bill Clinton on Wednesday sought the same kind of cash to help his Democratic Party get out of debt.

Clinton's undisguised straddle came at a dinner with four dozen top Democratic fund-raisers at the Mayflower Hotel. As he pitched for big contributions to help pay off the Democrats' $14.4 million debt, about 50 representatives of the citizens' lobby Common Cause marched in protest outside the hotel.

In a brief speech, Clinton made no direct appeal for money -- in fact the word never crossed his lips. Instead, he ticked off a list of administration accomplishments and spoke of the need to "put meat on the bones" of his policies.

"I believe you have helped to contribute to a profound, almost revolutionary positive change in the direction of our country," Clinton told the donors, who dined on grilled beef and salmon with a mixed green salad and parfait dessert.
Vice President Al Gore, who also attended the dinner, came closer to an outright appeal for funds to pay the party's debt and finance the 1998 mid-term congressional elections.
"More battles are yet to come," Gore said. "We need you, as you helped us win these last battles, to help us win these battles that are yet to come."

The White House initially said Clinton's appearance at the dinner would be off-limits to reporters because he would be discussing campaign strategy and did not want Republicans to find out about Democratic campaign plans for 1998.
But it was later decided to let the press cover Clinton's opening remarks.

It was understood that the dinner participants, who were not identified, would raise or give $250,000. That seemingly conflicts with a new Democratic National Committee policy to limit large donations to $100,000 a year.

The policy stems from the uproar over Clinton's campaign financing tactics in his 1996 bid for re-election, including offering big contributors overnight lodging in the historic Lincoln bedroom in the White House.

Democratic officials said the cap was not being violated because it is collecting money under a two-year programme in which individuals could give $100,000 this year, $100,000 next year and raise another $50,000 from other sources.
Asked why the Democrats were unwilling to release a list of names of the dinner guests, national chairman Steve Grossman said: "It's a matter of personal privacy."

"These are people coming together to have a substantive discussion about the future of the party. We think they're entitled to their privacy," Grossman said. "Any contributions they make will be filed in due course with the Federal Election Commission and be made a matter of public record."

The fund-raiser took place as federal and congressional investigations proceeded into Democratic money raising from last year's campaign cycle. Clinton has tried to blunt criticism by appealing for campaign finance reform.

In an effort to prod Congress to get moving on the issue, Clinton asked the FEC last week to issue a regulation outlawing "soft money" contributions. Republicans insisted only Congress could take such an action.

Under current regulations, wealthy donors, corporations and labour unions can get around federal limits of $1,000 to individual candidates by donating as much money as they want to the Republican or Democratic parties.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton was not being hypocritical in calling for a soft money ban and then solicting it. "We're not going to unilaterally concede the 1998 election to the Republican Party," he said.
